'''''Paradoxes of the Infinite''''' (German: ''Paradoxien des Unendlichen'') is a posthumously published treatise by the Bohemian philosopher, theologian and mathematician [[Bernard Bolzano]] (1781–1848). Edited by his former student [[František Přihonský]] and published in Leipzig in 1851, the book surveys “paradoxes” connected with the infinite in mathematics, geometry, physics and metaphysics, with the aim of showing that such paradoxes are not genuine contradictions once the relevant concepts are made precise. The work is often discussed in the prehistory of set theory for its detailed defence of actual (completed) infinity and its analysis of one-to-one pairings between infinite “multitudes” and their parts, themes later central to Dedekind’s and Cantor’s work on infinite collections.<ref>{{cite encyclopedia |last=Ferreirós |first=José |title=The Early Development of Set Theory |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |date=2025 |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/settheory-early/ |access-date=2025-12-05}}</ref><ref>{{cite encyclopedia |last=Spade |first=Paul Vincent |title=History of logic: Georg Cantor |encyclopedia=Encyclopædia Britannica |url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/history-of-logic/Georg-Cantor |access-date=2025-12-05}}</ref>

==Background and publication==
According to Přihonský’s editor’s preface, Bolzano began writing the book in 1847 while staying with the editor in Liboch (near Mělník) and completed it in the summer of 1848, the final year of his life.<ref name="Russ-Preface">{{cite book |last=Bolzano |first=Bernard |title=The Mathematical Works of Bernard Bolzano |editor-last=Russ |editor-first=Steve |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=Oxford |year=2004 |chapter=Editor’s Preface (''Paradoxes of the Infinite'')}}</ref> After receiving the manuscript from Bolzano’s heirs, Přihonský prepared it for publication by correcting passages, improving legibility, and supplying a detailed synopsis of contents; he dated his preface from Bautzen (Budissin) on 10 July 1850 and chose Leipzig partly for wider distribution.<ref name="Russ-Preface" /> The first edition appeared in 1851 with the Leipzig publisher C. H. Reclam.<ref>{{cite book |last=Bolzano |first=Bernard |title=Paradoxien des Unendlichen |editor-last=Přihonský |editor-first=František |location=Leipzig |publisher=C. H. Reclam |year=1851 |language=de}}</ref>

==Overview and structure==
The work is organised into 70 numbered sections. A synopsis supplied by the editor indicates the book’s main arc:<ref name="Russ-Contents">{{cite book |last=Bolzano |first=Bernard |title=The Mathematical Works of Bernard Bolzano |editor-last=Russ |editor-first=Steve |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=Oxford |year=2004 |chapter=Synopsis of contents (''Paradoxes of the Infinite'')}}</ref>
* §§1–19: competing conceptions of the infinite in mathematics and philosophy; the “objectivity” of the relevant concepts; and examples intended to motivate the existence of infinite multitudes (e.g., truths, numbers, quantities, and the divisibility of time and space).<ref name="Russ-Contents" />
* §§20–23: the “noteworthy relation” of pairing members of two infinite multitudes so that nothing remains unpaired (a one-to-one correspondence), and the resulting tension between equinumerosity and the part–whole intuition.<ref name="Russ-Contents" />
* §§24–37: “calculation with the infinite,” including discussion of the infinitely great and infinitely small, restrictions on the use of zero, and conditions under which infinite sums may be treated as equal.<ref name="Russ-Contents" />
* §§38–49: paradoxes tied to the continuum, and to time and space, including critical discussion of claims involving infinite magnitude or infinitesimal parts; examples include questions about infinite curvature and other “paradoxical relationships” of spatial extensions.<ref name="Russ-Contents" />
* §§50–70: paradoxes in physics and metaphysics, including arguments about individuation (e.g., denial that there are two “altogether equal” things) and related consequences for atomism and the structure of the physical world.<ref name="Russ-Contents" />

==Key themes==
===Actual infinity and the “harmlessness” of paradox===
Bolzano’s stated project is to treat paradoxes surrounding infinity as apparent rather than real contradictions. In later historical discussion, this is often described as a systematic defence of actual infinity within mathematics, combined with an attempt to clarify which principles of finite reasoning fail (or require modification) in infinite contexts.<ref name="FerreirósSEP">{{cite encyclopedia |last=Ferreirós |first=José |title=The Early Development of Set Theory |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |date=2025 |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/settheory-early/ |access-date=2025-12-05}}</ref>

===Collections, multitudes, and terminology===
Bolzano distinguishes several kinds of “collections” in the opening portions of the treatise, separating the general idea of a collection (''Inbegriff'') from the special case of a multitude (''Menge'') in which the arrangement of parts is treated as irrelevant. Modern commentators often translate ''Menge'' as “multitude” to avoid importing later Cantorian assumptions into Bolzano’s framework.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Trlifajová |first=Kateřina |title=Bolzano's Infinite Quantities |journal=Foundations of Science |year=2017 |volume=23 |issue=4 |pages=681–704 |doi=10.1007/s10699-018-9549-z |arxiv=1711.01603 }}</ref>

===One-to-one correspondence and the part–whole tension===
A central portion of the book analyses the possibility of pairing elements of two infinite multitudes so that each element of either multitude occurs in exactly one pair (what later mathematics calls a bijection). Bolzano notes that such a pairing can hold even when one multitude is (in an intuitive part–whole sense) contained in the other, and he argues that—unlike the finite case—pairing alone is not always sufficient to conclude “equality in respect of plurality.”<ref name="FerreirósSEP" /> He therefore appeals to additional conditions (often glossed as “determining grounds” or a shared “way of being formed”) to justify claims of equality or ratio for infinite multitudes in specific cases.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Trlifajová |first=Kateřina |title=Bolzano's Infinite Quantities |journal=Foundations of Science |year=2017 |volume=23 |issue=4 |pages=681–704 |doi=10.1007/s10699-018-9549-z |arxiv=1711.01603 }}</ref>

This stance is frequently contrasted with later nineteenth-century set theory, in which Dedekind and Cantor elevated one-to-one correspondence to a primary criterion for comparing sizes of infinite collections.<ref name="BritannicaCantor">{{cite encyclopedia |last=Spade |first=Paul Vincent |title=History of logic: Georg Cantor |encyclopedia=Encyclopædia Britannica |url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/history-of-logic/Georg-Cantor |access-date=2025-12-05}}</ref>

===Infinite quantities and infinite sums===
In the sections dealing with “calculation with the infinite,” Bolzano rejects a number of informal uses of infinitesimals and infinite magnitudes (including treating division by zero as meaningful), and attempts to state constraints under which operations involving infinitely small or large quantities can be made consistent.<ref name="Russ-Contents" /> Recent scholarship has re-examined these parts of the book, arguing that Bolzano’s mature views are best understood not as a precursor of Cantorian cardinal arithmetic but as a theory of infinite sums with its own algebraic structure.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bellomo |first1=Anna |last2=Massas |first2=Guillaume |title=Bolzano's Mathematical Infinite |journal=The Review of Symbolic Logic |volume=16 |issue=1 |date=2023 |pages=59–113 |doi=10.1017/S1755020321000010}}</ref>

==Reception and influence==
Bolzano’s book was published posthumously and (by some accounts) had limited immediate impact on the subsequent development of mathematics.<ref name="FerreirósSEP" /> Nevertheless, later writers in the history of logic and set theory have highlighted its role as an early, sustained attempt to analyse infinite collections and the principles governing their comparison.<ref name="FerreirósSEP" /> In particular, Encyclopædia Britannica notes that Dedekind and Cantor made explicit use of one-to-one mappings as a tool for “measuring” sets, and that Dedekind formulated a definition of an infinite set in terms of correspondence with a proper part—an idea closely related to the correspondences treated in ''Paradoxien des Unendlichen''.<ref name="BritannicaCantor" />

The book has also attracted attention in mathematics education and philosophy of mathematics as a historically rich source of arguments and examples about infinity, especially where intuitive part–whole reasoning conflicts with correspondence-based comparison.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Waldegg |first=Guillermo |title=Bolzano's Approach to the Paradoxes of Infinity: Implications for Teaching |journal=Science & Education |volume=14 |issue=8–9 |year=2005 |pages=679–702 |doi=10.1007/s11191-004-5290-3 |doi-broken-date=10 December 2025 }}</ref>
